vignette:
He is 25, a journalist early in his career, and before the trauma he describes himself as the kind of person who moved toward commotion rather than away from it. He grew up admiring reporters who stood in the middle of public events and helped other people make sense of them. He is in a steady relationship, close to his mother and two younger siblings, and proud of the life he is building in the city. When he talks about the months before the incident, he remembers being tired but energized, always chasing deadlines, carrying two phones, a recorder, and a notebook, telling his girlfriend that the work felt meaningful even when it was chaotic.

The event he returns to again and again happened while he was covering a public demonstration. He had gone there expecting tension, but not what followed. He remembers the day in fragments sharpened by fear: the heat rising from the road, people chanting, officers in riot gear forming a line, the metallic smell of dust and exhaust. He had his press card visible and his camera lifted. At first he was focused on getting names, quotes, and images. Then the crowd surged. He says it happened “too fast and too slowly at the same time.” He saw an officer strike a young man who had already fallen. He moved closer on instinct, filming, and shouted that he was press. An officer turned toward him, and the expression on the man’s face is something he still sees clearly at night—flat, almost bored. He was shoved to the ground, hit several times, and dragged toward a police vehicle while trying to protect his camera with his body. He remembers a boot pressing into his back, his cheek against the pavement, someone accusing him of provoking violence, someone else laughing. In the vehicle he felt certain, for several minutes that stretched endlessly, that they could make him disappear and no one would know where he had gone.

He was released later that day without charges, bruised and shaken, after colleagues and his editor began making calls. The physical injuries faded within weeks. He returned to work quickly, partly because he needed the income and partly because staying home felt like surrender. But almost immediately, he noticed that something in him had changed. On assignment he scans every street for uniforms, every parked truck for tinted windows. If he hears boots striking pavement or the crackle of a police radio, his body reacts before he can think; his chest tightens, his hands go numb, and his stomach drops as if he is back on the ground with weight on his back. He keeps his press card hidden now until the last possible moment, though he also fears not displaying it. Either choice feels dangerous.

At night he sleeps lightly, waking to dreams in which he is unable to speak while officers stand over him. Sometimes in the dream he tries to call his girlfriend, but his phone has no screen, or his fingers will not work. He wakes drenched in sweat and checks the locks two or three times before lying back down. His girlfriend tells him he jerks awake if she touches him unexpectedly. He feels ashamed of that. He says she used to know him as warm and playful; now she studies his face before entering a room.

In the newsroom he still produces strong work, but at a cost few people see. He sits where he can watch the entrance. He avoids stories involving police when he can, then despises himself for avoiding them. When an editor insists he attend a press briefing at police headquarters, he spends the morning nauseated, rehearsing exit routes instead of questions. He goes, because not going would be noticed, but while an officer speaks at the podium he stops hearing the words and focuses only on the officer’s belt, hands, and posture. Later he cannot write the story without repeatedly losing the thread. He reads his notes and finds gaps where his mind seemed to go blank.

He has become more withdrawn with friends. He declines invitations to crowded restaurants and hates sitting with his back to a door. Loud arguments in public make him flinch. He drinks more than he used to on weekends, telling himself it is the only way to quiet his mind enough to sleep. At the same time, he feels detached even in moments that should be easy: eating with his girlfriend, calling home, listening to music on the taxi ride to work. He often feels he is watching his life from a short distance away.

What troubles him most is not only fear, but the collapse of assumptions he once relied on. He became a journalist because he believed that witnessing offered some protection—that if events were documented, truth mattered. Since the assault, he is less certain. He keeps replaying the moment he identified himself and was hit anyway. He wonders whether the camera made him a target rather than a safeguard. He still goes out with a notebook and recorder, still asks questions, still files stories, but each assignment now carries an undercurrent of dread. He tells himself to stay sharp, stay useful, stay calm. Inside, he is braced as if the next blow could come at any time.
